findings.finding: NN/g's 2018 eyetracking study found users spent about 57% of page-viewing time above the fold and 74% in the first two screenfuls, down from 80% above the fold in 2010.
findings.number: 57% above the fold; 74% in first two screenfuls (80% in 2010)
findings.quote: In our most recent study, users spent about 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold.
findings.context: NN/g eyetracking: over 130,000 fixations from 120 participants on 1920x1080 screens, thousands of sites; compared with an earlier 1024x768 study from 2010.
findings.caveat: Desktop-size screens, attention (looking) not clicks; general websites, not SEO answer pages; no conversion data.
findings.implication: Put the first Dream Board link in the first screen or two beside the answer; a link only at the bottom reaches the minority who read that far.

findings.finding: On general websites more than 42% of viewing time fell in the top 20% of the page and more than 65% in the top 40%, whatever the page length.
findings.number: 42% of viewing time in top 20% of page; 65% in top 40%
findings.quote: On general websites, more than 42% of the viewing time fell within the top 20% of the page, and more than 65% of the time was spent in the top 40% of the page.
findings.context: Same NN/g 2018 eyetracking study (120 participants, over 130,000 fixations); pages were split into 20% segments so page length does not matter.
findings.caveat: Desktop screens; attention not clicks; general sites, not informational pages specifically.
findings.implication: On a long guide, a CTA at roughly 20 to 40% of page depth (right after the direct answer) sits where most attention is; a CTA in the last 30% sits where little is.

findings.finding: NN/g measured a sharp attention cliff at the fold: the 100 pixels just above the fold were viewed 102% more than the 100 pixels just below it.
findings.number: 102% more views just above than just below the fold (57,453 fixations)
findings.quote: Elements above the fold were seen more than elements below the fold: the 100 pixels just above the fold were viewed 102% more than the 100 pixels just below the fold.
findings.context: NN/g (Amy Schade, 2015) analysis of 57,453 eyetracking fixations across a wide range of pages, excluding search pages.
findings.caveat: 2015 desktop-era data; NN/g itself notes the fold differs by device, and on mobile the first screen is much shorter.
findings.implication: The first link should be visible on the first phone screen without scrolling and be repeated further down; do not rely on one link below the first screen.

findings.finding: Chartbeat (via TIME) reported that 66% of attention on a normal media page is spent below the fold, the opposite of the NN/g emphasis on the top.
findings.quote: Here’s the skinny, 66% of attention on a normal media page is spent below the fold.
findings.context: Chartbeat CEO Tony Haile, TIME, 2014; the article says Chartbeat looked at 2 billion visits across the web over a month. Read through the Internet Archive copy because time.com refuses curl.
findings.caveat: Analytics-vendor figure on news/media pages, method (engaged time) not printed on the page; secondhand relative to the underlying dataset; contradicts the top-heavy NN/g eyetracking result so the two are measuring different things.
findings.implication: Attention continues down a long page for people who stay, so a CTA after the answer (mid-page) and again after the last section is not wasted; do not rely on the top only.

findings.finding: Chartbeat found that 55% of visitors who click through spend fewer than 15 seconds actively on the page.
findings.quote: In fact, a stunning 55% spent fewer than 15 seconds actively on a page.
findings.context: Chartbeat, 2 billion visits over one month on publisher sites (TIME, 2014); the article adds that one in every three visitors spend less than 15 seconds reading article pages.
findings.caveat: News/media sites, 2014, analytics vendor, engaged-time definition not printed; informational wedding-fee pages may hold readers longer or shorter.
findings.implication: Assume half the visitors are gone in 15 seconds: the answer and the first Dream Board link must be on the first screen, not after the explanation.

findings.finding: Users read only about 20% of the text on an average web page, so a call to action that waits for the end of an article meets few readers.
findings.quote: More realistically, users will read about 20% of the text on the average page.
findings.context: Jakob Nielsen (2008) using the Weinreich et al. study: 25 users' browsers instrumented, data collected in 2005.
findings.caveat: Very old (2005 data) and small (25 users, whom Nielsen describes as above-average, several university employees); averages across all page types.
findings.implication: Keep the answer short and early and treat the end-of-page CTA as a safety net, not the main placement.

findings.finding: A sticky button at the bottom of a long mobile page (appearing after the user scrolls past the form, tapping scrolls back to it) beat the no-button control in every variation, by at least 8% in conversion and by up to 25% in sales.
findings.number: +8% minimum, +25% sales best variant (+22% revenue per visitor)
findings.quote: Every variation beat the no-button control by at least 8%.
findings.context: CRE client test on a long mobile product page for high-price products; four variations of a sticky bottom button vs a control with no sticky button.
findings.caveat: Agency win report: no sample size or significance printed; ecommerce product page not a free app; the lowest-commitment label ('Choose Size & Color') got the most clicks but fewer sales than 'Start Your Risk-Free Trial', so the most-clicked wording was not the best.
findings.implication: On phones, add a sticky bottom 'start your free Dream Board' button that appears after the first screen and scrolls back to or opens the quiz; test the label, not just the position.

findings.finding: A sticky header bar lifted donor conversion 13.1% on mobile only; the same bar lost 5% on desktop and 11% on tablet.
findings.quote: The second treatment, with the thank-you messaging, increased donor conversion by 13.1%—but only on mobile devices.
findings.context: NextAfter experiment for CaringBridge (nonprofit donation page): control vs two sticky header bars; total sample size 143,839; ran a little over a month plus ten days to reach validity.
findings.caveat: Donation page not an informational guide; the bar was a message header, not a button; vendor (NextAfter) documenting its own experiment; mobile result emerged only after segmenting.
findings.implication: Show any sticky element on phones only, and read results by device, because a bar that helps on a phone can hurt on a desktop.

findings.finding: On the Rock Content blog, moving an offer from the sidebar to a fixed footer bar raised the click rate by 50% (sidebar baseline 0.077% of page views), and over the full run more than doubled it.
findings.number: +50% click rate (0.077% sidebar baseline; 0.134% and 0.151% in later months)
findings.quote: Our results were better than expected, with a 50% increase in the click rate, instead of the estimated 10%.
findings.context: Blog post pages (informational content), one offer, 30 days of fixed bar compared with the preceding 30 days of sidebar, then two more monthly periods.
findings.caveat: NOT a simultaneous A/B split: the sidebar figures are retroactive data from the previous period; the metric is clicks per page view, not sign-ups; one site; vendor writing about its own blog. It does show the realistic scale: a blog-wide CTA clicks at roughly 0.08 to 0.15% of page views.
findings.implication: A fixed bar on guide pages is a plausible upgrade over a sidebar link, but expect clicks per page view in the low tenths of a percent, not several percent; measure it as clicks per page view.

findings.finding: On an article page an inline acquisition offer drew 2.0% clicks against 0.10% for a mid-roll ad banner in the same spot, 1,870.7% more offer clicks; NextAfter credits banner blindness.
findings.quote: The inline treatment increased the number of offer clicks by over 1,870%!
findings.context: NextAfter experiment on a high-traffic nonprofit website (article pages): mid-roll ad banner rotation vs an inline acquisition offer placed within the content; total sample size 242,062, confidence stated above 95%.
findings.caveat: Nonprofit email sign-up offer, not an app; the comparison is banner-styled vs inline-styled, so look and wording changed together; vendor documenting its own test; downstream conversion was not measured (the page lists 0% change in conversion rate and average gift).
findings.implication: Make the Dream Board link look like part of the article (an inline text link or content-style card after the answer), never a banner-style ad block.

findings.finding: HubSpot tested a slide-in CTA against the static CTA at the bottom of each post on ten of its highest-traffic posts: 192% higher click-through and 27% more submissions, although the slide-in converted a smaller share of clickers.
findings.quote: In this test, the slide- in CTA had a 192% higher CTR and generated 27% more submissions .
findings.context: HubSpot Marketing blog, one month, ten of HubSpot's highest-trafficked blog posts, slide-in vs static bottom-of-post CTA.
findings.caveat: Vendor testing its own product feature; no sample size or significance printed; the slide-in CTA had a lower conversion rate after the click, so the gain came from volume; the page's next sentence says submissions 'wasn't higher', which appears to mean per-click conversion rate (treat the 27% as HubSpot's headline figure); B2B lead forms, not a free app.
findings.implication: A bottom-of-page CTA is the weakest spot; a CTA that appears while the reader is mid-page (slide-in or sticky) gets far more clicks, but expect a lower share of those clicks to finish the quiz.

findings.finding: Unbounce analysed about 35,000 of its customers' landing pages and found video pages performed roughly as well or slightly worse than pages without video, on both mobile and desktop.
findings.number: approx. 35,000 pages (medians similar or lower with video; no percentages printed in the text)
findings.quote: This tells us that, overall, video appears to have a minimal or negative impact on the performance of a landing page—regardless of the conversion goal.
findings.context: Unbounce data analyst (Floss Taylor, 2021): about 35,000 Unbounce customer landing pages per time frame (late 2020 to early 2021) split into no video, embedded video and background video, by industry, channel and device.
findings.caveat: Observational (not randomised): pages with video differ from pages without; the effect sizes are in charts, no conversion rates are printed in the text; the page says some industries (real estate) were strongly negative.
findings.implication: A video is not a safe default: if we show the product, do it with a static or silent looping preview that costs no load time and test it against the plain button.

findings.finding: Crazy Egg's long homepage with a three-minute explainer video generated 64% more conversions than the control in a split test.
findings.quote: Even though the video’s message was similar to that of the rest of the page, during the split-test the version of the page with the video in it generated 64% more conversions than the control.
findings.context: CRE case study on Crazy Egg (an analytics SaaS): three-minute script, produced by Demo Duck, hosted on Wistia, tested with Google's split-testing tool on the homepage.
findings.caveat: Agency self-report: no sample size printed, and 'control' is not defined precisely (the same page says the earlier long page beat the control by 30%); one case; a 3-minute explainer for a paid SaaS, not a 90-second free quiz.
findings.implication: A short demo of what the visitor gets can lift conversions in a considered purchase, but it needs a real test on our own pages before we build video.

findings.finding: Vidyard's coming-soon email page converted 6.5% with no video, 11% with an embedded animated explainer (+69%) and 13% when the video opened in a lightbox on click (+100%).
findings.quote: Without video: (J) 6.5% average conversion rate With video embedded in page: (H) 11% average conversion rate (69% conversion lift) With video in lightbox modal popup: (D) 13% average conversion rate (100% conversion lift)
findings.context: Michael Litt of Vidyard, Oct 2011: an email-collection landing page built in Unbounce, three versions tested.
findings.caveat: Written by a video vendor; 2011; no sample size or significance printed; a 'coming soon' email-capture page, not an app; another vendor summary quotes different numbers (6% to 12%), so use the Unbounce original.
findings.implication: Where a demo is offered, letting a click open it in a lightbox beat an always-visible embed in this test, so keep the CTA button visible and put the preview behind or beside it.

findings.finding: Device Magic swapped its homepage video for a rotating image slider and got 35% more visitors reaching the sign-up page and 31% more sign-ups; the team suspected the video was too technical.
findings.quote: The image slider variation increased conversions from the home page to the sign-up page by 35% , and the total increase in subsequent sign-ups was 31% .
findings.context: VWO success story: Device Magic (mobile forms SaaS) tested its homepage with a video against a jQuery image slider; the control led early and the result inverted after more data.
findings.caveat: Vendor (VWO) summary of a customer test, no visitor counts printed; the video's quality was suspected to be poor, so this is not 'images beat video' in general; early look was the opposite.
findings.implication: Still images of the actual output (a short slide of boards and matching dresses) can beat a mediocre video; run any test long enough because the early lead flipped.

findings.finding: Felix + Iris changed its hero to a picture of the actual free home try-on kit, added three plain steps (take the quiz, see recommended frames, try them free) and relabelled the button 'Start Fit Profile', lifting conversions 71.62%.
findings.quote: Treatment #2, with its clear CTA as well as more relevant hero image with step-by-step details of the process laid out, increased conversion 71.62% with a 95% level of confidence.
findings.context: Felix + Iris (prescription eyewear), homepage hero for starting a free quiz-led home try-on; control vs Treatment 1 (new hero image plus steps, same 'Get Started' button) vs Treatment 2 (same plus 'Start Fit Profile'); the interviewee mentions quick three-day tests.
findings.caveat: Several changes bundled (image, steps, button label); the page does not print Treatment 1's result or the visitor count; MECLABS write-up of a company's own test; new brand with no brand equity.
findings.implication: Closest analogue to Dream Board: show the thing she receives, list the 3 steps in plain words, and name the button after the action ('Start my Dream Board'), then test them together.

findings.finding: A web.dev case study of a Vodafone landing-page A/B test found the version with a 31% better Largest Contentful Paint generated 8% more sales, a reminder that anything heavy on the first screen (video, big animation) has a cost.
findings.quote: By running an A/B test on a landing page (where version A was optimized for Web Vitals and had a 31% better LCP score in the field than version B), Vodafone determined that optimizing for Web Vitals generated 8% more sales.
findings.context: web.dev case study (March 2021): Vodafone A/B test on a landing page, version A optimised for Web Vitals vs version B.
findings.caveat: Single telecom test; the page does not print visitor counts; it measures page speed, not video, so applying it to video is an inference.
findings.implication: Do not add autoplay video or heavy animation above the answer; if we show a preview use a lightweight image or compressed looping clip loaded after the first screen.

findings.finding: Google's web.dev shows how big the cost of animation formats is: the same looping animation is 3.7 MB as a GIF, 551 KB as MP4 and 341 KB as WebM.
findings.number: 3.7 MB GIF vs 551 KB MP4 vs 341 KB WebM
findings.quote: In this example, the initial GIF is 3.7 MB, compared to the MP4 version, which is 551 KB, and the WebM version, which is only 341 KB!
findings.context: web.dev tutorial (2018): one example animation converted with FFmpeg; recommends <video autoplay loop muted playsinline> to replace GIFs.
findings.caveat: One example file, not an average; it is file size, not a conversion measurement.
findings.implication: If we use a looping demo of the quiz next to the button, serve it as muted WebM/MP4, never a GIF.

findings.finding: Wistia reports that calls to action inside its customers' videos convert at about 16% on average, and for videos under one minute the best CTA position is the first quarter of the video.
findings.number: ~16% average video CTA conversion; 36,000+ CTAs analysed
findings.quote: Video CTAs have an average conversion rate of about 16% across the Wistia platform.
findings.context: Wistia analysis of over 36,000 CTAs in Wistia-hosted videos in 2024; the page does not define 'conversion' but it appears to be clicks on the in-video CTA.
findings.caveat: Vendor data on its own platform; the denominator is viewers who saw the CTA, not all page visitors (most visitors never press play).
findings.implication: If we make a short demo, put the Dream Board button inside the first quarter of the video as well as on the page, but do not treat 16% as a page-level rate.

no_evidence: CTA repetition (how many CTAs per informational page): no controlled A/B test with a number found; the only source (an agency write-up of 100+ tests) gives no sample sizes or effect sizes.

Published A/B test of a sticky HEADER button on an informational/SEO content page (not ecommerce, not donation): none found with a usable number (an Instapage customer story claims +40% on 1,900 visitors but is a vendor page with no significance; left out).

NN/g on video vs text or autoplay for conversion: the NN/g Video Usability article (2014) is qualitative only, no numbers; no NN/g number on informational images and conversion (Photos as Web Content gives fixation counts, not conversions).
Controlled A/B test of a product SCREENSHOT or looping animation next to a CTA on a content page: none found with a printed lift; screenshot-versus-stock claims are guides without test data.
HubSpot's '121% more conversions for anchor-text CTAs vs banner CTAs' is widely repeated, but I could not find HubSpot's original page; only secondary copies (not usable).
GoodUI pattern pages (Sticky Call To Action, 29 tests) hide the effect sizes behind a membership wall; no usable number.
Baymard and CXL: no CTA-placement or video conversion numbers found on their pages (CXL's above-the-fold article is behind Cloudflare and was not readable).
Mobile-specific scroll-depth benchmark: Contentsquare and eMarketer pages are blocked or give no mobile figure; NN/g's scroll numbers are from 1920x1080 desktop screens.
notes: All quotes were copied from pages opened with curl and are in /Users/olivier/Documents/rachels-list-guides/.cache/raw/conv/r1/ (text dumps). The Chartbeat/TIME numbers are read from an Internet Archive copy because time.com returns HTTP 406 to curl; the quote is TIME's own text. Contradiction to know: NN/g says attention is top-heavy (57% above the fold) while Chartbeat says 66% of attention is below the fold; they measure different things (eye fixations vs engaged time on news pages), so the safe design is a link on the first screen AND later on the page. Not used because confounded or secondhand: CRE's Moz case (+52% sales, >5,000 visitors) changed page length, headline and video together; Crazy Egg 64% is similarly an agency self-report. The ION/Rock Content +50% is a before/after on the same blog, not a split test. Wistia, Unbounce, HubSpot, NextAfter, CRE, VWO, MarketingExperiments are vendors publishing their own results; NN/g and Google web.dev are independent. Most useful single result for the Dream Board is Felix + Iris (quiz-led free kit: show the kit, three steps, action-named button, +71.62%), but it bundles three changes.
